case_brief.incident_description: Lerato was a regional sales coordinator employed for three years. In August she was told that her sales figures were below target. She says the targets had been increased by 35% while two vacancies in her team remained unfilled. She was never placed on a formal performance improvement plan. She had two coaching meetings over three weeks but no written improvement plan, no agreed milestones and no additional resources. She was dismissed for poor performance after the second coaching meeting.
case_brief.original_client_narrative: My targets went up 35 percent while we were two people short. They called two meetings coaching but I never got a PIP or clear plan. Three weeks later they fired me for poor performance.
case_brief.recommended_next_step: WP letter challenging the adequacy of the performance-management process and the fairness of dismissal.
weaknesses: Employer had raised performance concerns before dismissal

letter:
Background

1. We are instructed by our client, Ms Lerato Ndlovu, in connection with the termination of her employment with Brightline Retail SA (Pty) Ltd on 28 October 2026. This letter is written on a without prejudice and subject to contract basis and nothing in it may be construed as an admission of fact or liability on the part of our client. Our client's rights to pursue this matter before the Commission for Conciliation, Mediation and Arbitration or any other competent forum are expressly reserved and are not affected by the sending of this letter or by any response to it.

2. Our client was employed as a Regional Sales Coordinator and, on her account, had been in the role for a period in the region of three years at the time of her dismissal. In or around August 2026 our client was informed that her sales targets had been increased by approximately 35%. On our client's account, two vacancies within her team remained unfilled throughout this period, so that the increased targets were to be achieved with reduced staffing capacity relative to the standard against which the targets were presumably set.

3. Our client reports that no standards review or documented performance improvement plan was put in place following the August 2026 target increase. Rather, our client attended two coaching meetings over a period of approximately three weeks. To the extent that the employer's records differ as to the content or formality of these meetings, our client's position is that no written improvement plan, no agreed milestones and no additional resources were provided at or following either meeting. Our client was dismissed for poor performance shortly after the second of these two meetings, on 28 October 2026.

Legal Claims

1. Unfair dismissal: poor performance under section 188(1) of the LRA: Our client's dismissal falls to be assessed under section 188(1) of the Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995, which requires that a dismissal be both substantively and procedurally fair. Where the stated reason for dismissal is poor performance, the Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025 sets out at paragraphs 19 and 20 the standard expected of an employer before it may fairly terminate employment on this ground. That standard requires that the performance standard applied be reasonable, that the employee be given a fair and genuine opportunity to meet it, and that any shortfall be properly attributed to the employee rather than to circumstances outside the employee's control. On our client's account, the sales targets against which her performance was measured were increased by approximately 35% while two positions in her team remained vacant. A target increase of this scale, applied without corresponding resourcing, raises a material question as to whether the standard set was reasonable in the circumstances or whether any shortfall against it is properly attributable to our client at all. This goes directly to the substantive fairness enquiry under paragraph 19 of the Code. Turning to the procedural dimension, paragraph 20 of the Code contemplates that an employee facing dismissal for poor performance ordinarily be given a structured and meaningful opportunity to improve, typically through a formal performance improvement plan with agreed milestones, appropriate support or resources, and a follow-up evaluation before any decision to dismiss is taken. On our client's account she was not placed on any formal performance improvement plan. She attended two coaching meetings over approximately three weeks, without a documented plan, without agreed milestones and without additional resources being made available to address the resourcing shortfall she had raised. A period of this length, without the structured elements contemplated by paragraph 20, falls materially short of the standard the Code anticipates and is unlikely to constitute the fair opportunity to improve that the law requires before a poor performance dismissal is fair.

Without Prejudice Settlement Proposal

Without any admission of liability and in the interests of resolving this matter efficiently and amicably, our client proposes the following terms of settlement. This proposal is made on a without prejudice and subject to contract basis and is intended to reflect a commercially sensible resolution calibrated to the litigation risk identified above, rather than to constitute any concession as to the matters in dispute.

• Compensation on an ex gratia, total cost to company basis. In light of the cumulative procedural defects identified above, together with the disputed substantive basis for dismissal and the safety context giving rise to the allegation, our client's position is that settlement should be calibrated toward the higher end of the compensation range available under section 194(1) of the LRA, being up to twelve months' remuneration

• Payment of ex gratia compensation to our client on a total cost to company basis, calculated with reference to the compensation available under section 194(1) of the LRA, up to a maximum of twelve months' remuneration, calibrated toward the higher end of that range in light of the absence of a formal performance improvement plan, the compressed and unstructured nature of the three-week improvement period afforded, and the unresolved question as to whether the performance standard applied was reasonable given the unfilled vacancies in our client's team

• Payment in lieu of notice calculated by reference to the applicable notice period under section 37 of the BCEA, subject to any more favourable contractual notice entitlement, with payment made in accordance with section 38 of the BCEA

• Payment of any accrued and untaken leave pay owed to our client under section 40 of the BCEA

• Written confirmation that any pension or provident fund contributions due in respect of our client's employment are paid up to date, and that the accumulated benefit will be dealt with in accordance with the rules of the applicable fund

• Written confirmation that UIF contributions have been paid up to date, together with a completed UI-19 certificate to enable our client to access unemployment benefits

• A certificate of service issued in terms of section 42 of the BCEA

• An agreed reference, in terms to be agreed between the parties, reflecting our client's role and tenure in neutral or positive terms

• A written undertaking that Brightline Retail SA (Pty) Ltd and its representatives will not disparage our client to any current or prospective employer or third party

• An undertaking of confidentiality as to the terms of any settlement, the fact and content of the underlying negotiations and the dispute itself, as between the parties and their respective advisers

• The settlement to be recorded in a formal written settlement agreement signed by both parties, with all of our client's rights reserved in full until such agreement is signed

Our client's compensatory exposure in this matter falls to be assessed against the cap of twelve months' remuneration available under section 194(1) of the LRA, having regard to the absence of a structured improvement process and the questions raised as to the reasonableness of the performance standard applied in circumstances of unfilled vacancies. We consider that a negotiated resolution at this stage serves both parties better than protracted proceedings before the CCMA, and our client remains open to a sensible commercial discussion on that basis.

We look forward to receiving your substantive response within seven calendar days of the date of this letter. Should no satisfactory response be received within that period, our client's rights to refer this dispute to the CCMA, or any other forum of competent jurisdiction, for determination will be exercised without further notice. All of our client's rights in this regard are expressly reserved.

criteria.problem: The settlement terms paragraph invents a 'safety context giving rise to the allegation' that does not appear anywhere in the case brief, which concerns only a poor performance dismissal with no safety or OHSA element. This is a fabricated fact injected into the settlement rationale and repeated in substance via 'cumulative procedural defects' framing that overstates the single procedural weakness (no PIP) into plural defects not separately established.
criteria.required_fix: Remove the invented 'safety context' reference entirely; ground the settlement calibration only in the confirmed facts (no PIP, three-week improvement period, 35% target increase against unfilled vacancies).
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "together with the disputed substantive basis for dismissal and the safety context giving rise to the allegation, our client's position is that settlement should be calibrated toward the higher end"

criteria.problem: The core poor-performance analysis correctly ties facts to the Code paragraphs 19-20 framework and to section 188(1), and reflects the HIGH merit band reasonably well. However, the fabricated safety reference in settlement terms misaligns the settlement narrative with the actual legal basis in the brief (poor performance only, no safety ground), and the settlement clause's compensation rationale is duplicated almost verbatim across two separate bullet points, diluting rather than sharpening the risk-to-value connection required for a HIGH-merit matter.
criteria.required_fix: Collapse the duplicated compensation bullets into a single clause, remove the safety reference, and ensure the calibration narrative cites only the confirmed procedural and substantive weaknesses (absence of PIP, compressed three-week period, 35% target increase with unfilled vacancies).
criteria.evidence_from_draft: Two settlement bullets both open with near-identical 'Compensation on an ex gratia, total cost to company basis' and 'Payment of ex gratia compensation... calibrated toward the higher end' language, and the first includes the unrelated safety reference.

criteria.problem: Tone is generally professional and restrained, consistent with counterparty-facing register. Minor issues: 'To the extent that the employer's records differ as to the content or formality of these meetings' is a reasonable conditional formulation, but the overall body reads slightly formulaic in the settlement section due to the repeated compensation bullets, which undercuts the 'confident but proportionate' standard by appearing padded rather than precise.
criteria.required_fix: Tighten settlement language to avoid repetition; vary sentence structure to remove the padded effect.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: Two near-duplicate compensation clauses in settlement_terms.

criteria.problem: The duplication of the ex gratia compensation clause across two separate settlement_terms entries is a clear structural defect (duplicated template content), contrary to the requirement for no duplicated content. Otherwise the background-to-claims-to-settlement progression is coherent and the single legal claim heading is concise and substantively tied to the facts.
criteria.required_fix: Merge the two compensation-related settlement bullets into one clause in the standing 3A.10 order (ex gratia compensation first, then notice, leave, etc.).
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "Compensation on an ex gratia, total cost to company basis..." followed immediately by "Payment of ex gratia compensation to our client on a total cost to company basis..." as two separate numbered settlement terms.

criteria.problem: The response window is correctly capped at seven calendar days and most clauses follow the standing 3A.10 order. However, the duplicated and fabricated-context compensation clause undermines actionability and commercial usability because a recipient reviewing this letter would see an internally inconsistent and seemingly padded compensation ask, and the settlement rationale references a ground (safety) not otherwise pleaded in the letter, creating confusion about the actual basis for the demand.
criteria.required_fix: Consolidate into one clear, well-calibrated ex gratia compensation clause tied solely to the pleaded poor-performance claim, remove the safety reference, retain the seven-day window.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: Duplicate compensation bullets; "safety context giving rise to the allegation" with no corresponding allegation or claim anywhere else in the draft.

criteria.problem: Mandatory current-law checks are largely satisfied: the Code is correctly cited as 'Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025' (not Schedule 8), no case law is cited, no rand figures appear, and the notice-pay clause correctly treats BCEA s37 (notice period) and s38 (payment instead of notice) as complementary rather than alternative ('calculated by reference to... section 37... with payment made in accordance with section 38'), which is correct. The non-disparagement clause is correctly one-way against the employer. However, the fabricated 'safety context giving rise to the allegation' is an unsupported invented fact that is itself a drafting-compliance problem (introducing a ground/allegation not in the brief), and the duplicated compensation clauses constitute a drafting defect under the 'no duplicated template content' requirement that also touches compliance with clean settlement-clause structure under 3A.10.
criteria.required_fix: Delete the invented safety reference and merge duplicate compensation clauses into a single clause consistent with 3A.10 ordering.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "the safety context giving rise to the allegation" with no supporting allegation elsewhere in the draft; duplicate ex gratia compensation bullets.

what_is_strong: The opening background paragraphs correctly use conditional/attributive language ('on our client's account') to distinguish the Client's account from confirmed fact, consistent with the drafting discipline required for contested matters.

The single legal claim is well-constructed: it correctly anchors the analysis in the current Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025 paragraphs 19-20, ties the 35% target increase and unfilled vacancies to the reasonableness-of-standard question, and ties the absence of a formal PIP and the three-week window to the procedural fairness enquiry, directly reflecting the brief's scoring_breakdown drivers.
The notice-pay clause correctly treats BCEA section 37 and section 38 as complementary rather than alternative mechanisms, avoiding a common drafting error.
The non-disparagement undertaking is correctly drafted as one-way against the employer, consistent with the Employee-side convention and the absence of any mutuality authorisation in the brief.
The response window is correctly capped at seven calendar days and the reservation-of-rights language is appropriately unhedged.
what_needs_work: The reference to a 'safety context giving rise to the allegation' in the first settlement bullet is fabricated; nothing in the case brief involves a safety issue or a disciplinary 'allegation' of any kind, since this is a poor-performance dismissal.

The ex gratia compensation term is duplicated almost verbatim across two separate settlement_terms entries, which is a structural defect under the 'no duplicated template content' requirement and under the standing settlement-clause order at 3A.10.

The settlement calibration language ('cumulative procedural defects', 'disputed substantive basis') slightly overstates the record, since the brief identifies one clear procedural gap (no PIP) and one substantive concern (target/resourcing mismatch), not a cumulative multiplicity of distinct procedural defects.

The conclusion paragraph's reference to 'questions raised as to the reasonableness of the performance standard' is fine, but the overall settlement framing would benefit from tighter, non-repetitive language connecting the specific HIGH-merit drivers to the calibration level.

forensic_questions: Can the Client confirm the exact wording or substance of any communication raising the 35% target increase, to establish whether it was communicated in writing or verbally and by whom?

Did the Client raise the resourcing shortfall (unfilled vacancies) directly with her manager during either coaching meeting, and if so, is there any written record (email, minutes) of that exchange?
Is there any documentary record (calendar invite, meeting notes, email) of the two coaching meetings that could corroborate the absence of a formal PIP or milestones?

What was the Client's gross monthly remuneration and full employment history (exact start date) to properly calibrate the notice, leave and severance entitlements referenced in the settlement clauses?
